(1) the proposed procedures are superior to some of the existing procedures in the literature, and (2) batching can be a useful strategy in some cases, but not in all.

In summary, our research is concerned with

the development of sequential procedures for the selection of the best system from a set of alternatives, when the expected performance of each simulated system is to be estimated from repeated sampling.
the development of a fully sequential procedure for selecting the best of a finite number, k, of simulated systems.

the development of sequential selection procedures that are robust to non-normality, that are efficient in terms of the number of observations required to select the best or near best system, and that are easy to use in practice.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
, for the problem of selecting the best system, the new procedures we present are superior to existing ones, in terms of the expected sample size, in most cases.

the proposed sequential procedures are the best available for selecting the best system from a finite set of simulated systems.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
, for the case of unequal variances, we have developed procedures that are more efficient than the existing procedures for selecting the maximum or the minimum of a finite number.
, in many cases, the new procedure can reduce the number of simulation runs needed to select the best or near best of a finite number.
the procedures we propose have good theoretical properties, and they perform well in practice.
The main takeaway from our work is that
, in many cases, it is better to select the best system by using small batches of data than by using a single large batch.
, for many practical problems, the procedures we develop are superior to existing procedures.
